newsitem.title: CHINA: China slips mysterious passenger out of country.
newsitem.headline: China slips mysterious passenger out of country.

text.p: Chinese aircraft on Tuesday spirited a mysterious passenger out of the country amid reports of an end to a crisis that stranded a top North Korean leader in rival Seoul's Beijing mission for nearly five weeks.

Chinese police maintained tight guard around the South Korean consular offices where North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum on February 12, despite reports that the most senior leader to flee Pyongyang had already left.
Chinese and South Korean officials, bombarded by questions on whether Hwang's Beijing sojourn had finally ended, declined all comment.

But a Seoul Foreign Ministry official said South Korea would make an announcement about Hwang on Tuesday. Seoul had earlier said an announcement would be made once Hwang landed in a third country after leaving China.
A China Southern Airlines flight carrying a mysterious VIP passenger took off on Tuesday morning from the southeastern city of Xiamen, bound for the Philippines.

The passenger had earlier taken a special dawn flight from a Beijing military airport, his route matching the one Hwang was expected to take when he ended weeks of diplomatic limbo at the centre of a crisis between China and the two rival Koreas.
"I can't say if (Hwang) is on board," said one airline official in Xiamen shortly after China Southern Flight CZ379 took off from the port city for the two-hour flight to Manila.
"And even if he is on board I wouldn't tell you," the official said.
Flight CZ379 had taken off nearly 40 minutes late, at 10.58 a.m. (0258 GMT), but this was not unusual, the official said.
In South Korea, Yonhap Television News quoted a government source as saying Hwang, the architect of North Korea's ruling ideology of strict self-reliance, had left Beijing.

Japan's Fuji Television said unmarked vehicles were used on Monday night to slip him past reporters waiting outside the tight police cordon around Seoul's consular compound in Beijing's tree-lined diplomatic quarter.

Pyongyang's top ideological theoretician spent the night at the military airport on the outskirts of Beijing before being flown out of the Chinese capital, the station said. Security remained strict on Tuesday morning around the South Korean consular office, where paramilitary police armed with assault rifles and backed by armoured personnel carriers have kept round-the-clock watch throughout Hwang's stay.
A South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to comment on reports that Hwang had left Beijing, saying China and Seoul would announce his departure after he left.
On Monday, a senior South Korean official said Hwang would stay in a third country "for a considerable period of time" before coming to South Korea.
A Philippine Foreign Ministry spokesman told Reuters the ministry would make a statement on Tuesday afternoon after being swamped with queries on whether Hwang was on his way.

Hwang's Beijing defection had muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War, and forced Beijing to choose between a new capitalist friend in the South and an old communist ally in the North.

North Korea at first accused Seoul of kidnapping the scholarly ideologue and sent scores of diplomats and students to keep vigil around his refuge, but the Stalinist hermit nation later appeared to ease its stance on the crisis.
